intro: Introduction to European Union Law. Lecture three: the institutions, part two — the Council, the Parliament, and the other bodies.

slides.13: Coreper and the A and B points — the Council's real working machinery. Coreper, the Committee of Permanent Representatives, meets in two formations: Coreper One, the deputies, handles the more technical files; Coreper Two, the ambassadors, the politically sensitive ones. It sorts the agenda into two kinds of item: A points, adopted in the Council without further discussion because agreement was reached below; and B points, actually debated by the ministers. Roughly two hundred and fifty working groups of civil servants feed into this. The practical lesson: most Union legislation is settled before any minister sees it.
slides.16: Decision-making, in overview. The presence quorum is a simple majority of voting members. For decisions, qualified majority is the standard, with simple majority, super-qualified majority and unanimity as the other thresholds. The figures come next, and the exam does ask for them.
slides.24: The Parliament's composition after the 2024 election, given as a seat distribution by political group.
slides.26: Political groups. Members of the European Parliament sit by political direction, not by nationality, and they are seated in the chamber from left to right accordingly. A group needs twenty-three members drawn from at least seven member states, and nobody may belong to two groups. Each group organises itself with a chair, a board and a secretariat, and decides its position by internal discussion — but here is the point that matters constitutionally: there is no group discipline. Members cannot be compelled to vote a particular way.
slides.50: Four roles of interest groups, sorted by the function each performs. As lobby, in the pluralist sense. As consultants or experts — through open consultation during policy preparation, and targeted consultation in working groups, which is the elite model. As co-decision-makers — through the Social Dialogue between trade unions and employers, and through voluntary agreements concluded with the Commission. And as supervisory actors — through complaints, lawsuits and protest. The third is the one that surprises: in Union social policy, the social partners can produce agreements that become law.
